newsitem.title: JAPAN: Scandal-hit Nomura, DKB pledge clean hands.
newsitem.headline: Scandal-hit Nomura, DKB pledge clean hands.

text.p: Japan's top brokerage and one of its biggest banks apologised on Friday for a scandal involving payoffs to the underworld and promised their shareholders they would be better corporate citizens in the future.

Nomura Securities Ltd and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank were two of the more than 2,000 Japanese companies which held shareholders' meetings on Friday, but the spotlight was focused on them because of the high-profile scandal involving payoffs to "sokaiya", or racketeers.
"We...will endeavour to firmly cut ties with anti-social elements such as sokaiya," Nomura President Junichi Ujiie told the brokerage's shareholders.

"We sincerely apologise... Former top executives of our company are suspected to have been involved in the crime which should not have occurred," said Ujiie, who assumed his post in May after a sweeping management shake-up sparked by the scandal.

Outgoing Dai-Ichi Kangyo president Katsuhiko Kondo told the bank's shareholders: "No matter what else changes, the foundation of a bank is its credibility. We are quite ashamed of having hurt the credibility of our bank."

Sokaiya, often but not always linked to crime syndicates, buy shares in firms and try to extort money from them by threatening to expose dubious business practices or stir up trouble at shareholders' meetings, which firms anyway regard as more of a ceremony than a forum for briefing investors.
Japan's Commercial Code has since 1983 banned payoffs to sokaiya, but many firms have found it tough to end the ties.

In the latest development, Jiji news agency reported on Friday that prosecutors had began questioning Tadashi Okuda and Kuniji Miyazaki, both former Dai-Ichi Kangyo chairmen, about their roles in the affair.

That follows the indictment on Thursday of four former executives of Dai-Ichi Kangyo on charges of making loans of 11.78 billion yen ($103 million) to Ryuichi Koike, the racketeer at the centre of the scandal.
They were the first Dai-Ichi Kangyo executives to be indicted.

Prosecutors also re-arrested Koike and his brother on Thursday on suspicion of receiving 320 million yen ($2.8 million) in cash from Nomura. The money was supposedly paid to the two for their pledge to ensure a smooth proceeding of Nomura's shareholders' meeting in 1995.

In an effort to improve its image in the wake of the scandal, Nomura posted a summary of its shareholders' meeting on the Internet, while Dai-Ichi Kangyo opened up its meeting to the media through television monitors placed at its headquarters.

A record 855 shareholders turned out for Nomura's gathering on Friday, topping the previous record of 542 who attended Nomura's annual meeting in 1991. That was when the brokerage was entangled in another huge scandal over links to gangsters and improper compensation to favoured clients.
Nomura's shareholders' meeting lasted more than three hours, making it the longest such event in recent years.
Dai-Ichi Kangyo's meeting, which lasted about 90 minutes compared with only 27 minutes last year, also ended without incident or any apparent attempt by sokaiya to interrupt it.
The bank earlier this month announced a massive management shake-up, including the resignation of 21 of its 40 directors to improve its image.
Katsuyuki Sugita, a Dai-Ichi Kangyo managing director who was to take over as the bank's president after the meeting, said: "The new management will completely reject any request from racketeers."
Kondo apologised to shareholders for causing them trouble because of the scandal, but acknowledged that the bank still had 7.5 billion yen ($65.7 million) of loans outstanding to racketeers.

Prosecutors last week charged Nomura president Hideo Sakamaki with illegal payoffs totalling 49.73 million yen ($436,000) to Koike and served him with a fresh arrest warrant on suspicion of paying him another 320 million yen ($2.80 million) on a separate occasion.

Nomura said on Friday that it would consider filing a damage suit against Sakamaki, who stepped down in March when the scandal broke, as well as against two other former executives accused of conspiring with him over the payoffs. ($1=114 yen)
